How it works

The science behind the stage.

Perigee combines NASA’s catalog of asteroid close approaches, JPL Horizons positions for each asteroid, and CelesTrak orbit data for satellites. It’s an educational explorer, not a NASA product or an impact-warning tool.

What you’re looking at

  • The forecast and asteroid catalog list each asteroid’s predicted closest approach in the 30-day window, from NASA NeoWs. A row is an event, not the object’s current location.
  • The stage shows where objects are at the displayed UTC time, on one true linear scale. Asteroid positions come from JPL Horizons; only asteroids inside the chosen distance appear.
  • Satellites share the same scale, so from far out they sit within a few pixels of Earth: zoom toward Earth, or pick a satellite distance, to see them. Positions are computed in your browser with the SGP4 model from CelesTrak orbit elements, used only within seven days of each element set. They’re predictions, not live tracking.
  • Paths show an asteroid’s next 30 days relative to Earth, or one orbit ahead for a satellite.

Scale and markers

  • Earth, the Moon and the Sun are drawn to scale. When Earth or the Moon is too small to see, a ring and label mark it.
  • Asteroid dots are enlarged; their size follows NASA’s estimated diameter on a compressed scale, and hollow means unknown. Satellite dots are a fixed size and colored by group.
  • One lunar distance (LD) ≈ 384,400 km.

Using the controls

  • Drag to rotate. Click the view first, then scroll or pinch to zoom. Arrow keys, +/− and Home also work.
  • The time bar and Play move every position together. Live follows the current time; Now returns to it.
  • Select anything for an At a glance summary and a Deep dive with the full numbers.

Classification and imagery

“Potentially hazardous” is NASA’s classification based on orbit and size. It is not an impact probability; see NASA’s definition and Sentry impact monitoring. Photos come from small reviewed lists, labeled as photographs or illustrations and as this object or the same type of spacecraft. Other asteroid matches from NASA’s archive are labeled unverified. All imagery is historical, not a live camera.

Freshness

Waiting for the data source.

The catalog refreshes every 15 minutes while Live is on. If NASA is unavailable, a dated saved snapshot is shown and labeled. Earth imagery: NASA Blue Marble (Reto Stöckli) and night lights (NASA Earth Observatory / Suomi NPP VIIRS). Moon: NASA SVS / LRO. Blue Marble source · Night-light source
